name: react-to-figma

# React to Figma

## Source of truth and boundaries

The requested React Web and React Native code is the source of truth for behavior and appearance; Figma is the destination. This workflow is code-first: it can create a new component or modify an existing one from the user's requirements, comparable Trilogy components, and the project's architecture, without requiring an existing Figma component or a Figma design first. Once the code is implemented and verified, create its Figma component if missing or update it if present. For a request solely to sync existing code, keep implementation and behavior unchanged unless the user also requests a code change; still add or update missing or stale JSDoc and required colocated documentation. Do not use a Figma-to-React workflow as a prerequisite for code creation.

Creating or modifying code authorizes the scoped implementation, types, exports, styles, tests, stories, and documentation needed for the request. Reuse existing semantic tokens; follow the shared style and Figma skills for missing tokens or generated files. Preserve unrelated local changes and functionality. Code Connect is suspended: do not create, modify, publish, or inspect mappings or `.figma.ts` files unless the user explicitly reactivates Code Connect in a later request.

## Procedure

1. Identify the requested component, determine whether the user asks to create, modify, or only sync it, and inspect comparable Trilogy components. For an existing component, inspect its types, exports, Web and Native implementations, subcomponents, SCSS styles, helpers, theme, tokens, stories, and tests. If several existing components match, ask which one to use. Load and follow [Trilogy Component Architecture](../trilogy-component-architecture/SKILL.md), [Trilogy Component JSDoc](../trilogy-component-jsdoc/SKILL.md), [Trilogy Styles and Tokens](../trilogy-styles-tokens/SKILL.md), and [Trilogy Component Tests](../trilogy-component-tests/SKILL.md).
   - For creation or modification, implement the requested behavior and visuals in React Web and Native based on the request, available references, existing components, and project conventions. Create or update public subcomponents (each in its own folder with its own `<name>.types.ts`, `index.ts`, styles, tests, and `docs.md`; never put a subcomponent's types in the parent's or a root-level types file; a prop with several possible values is a string `enum` there, never a union of string literals, as the architecture skill defines), types, exports, semantic styles, tests, stories, JSDoc, and colocated `docs.md` as needed. Do not require Figma to exist or be accessible before beginning the code phase. Preserve existing behavior and ask before incompatible or unspecified functional changes.
   - For sync-only work, analyze code as it stands without changing implementation, types, behavior, styles, tests, or stories unnecessarily. Add missing colocated documentation and correct stale or missing JSDoc for public components as required by the shared skills.
   - For each requested family, recursively inspect its `index.ts` barrel, subcomponent folders, types, public exports, and usage examples. Explicitly inventory the main component and every public subcomponent, even when the parent does not render it automatically. For example, `Alert` includes `AlertContent`, `AlertTitle`, and `AlertDescription`; `Button` includes `ButtonList`. These names are examples, not an exhaustive list.
   - A family request includes its public subcomponents by default: find, create, or update each on the family's Figma page unless explicitly excluded. Do not treat unexported internal components as public by default. Do not recreate an existing mapping or modify an external library without authorization.
   - Keep component documentation in colocated Markdown. If adding a missing docs page for a requested public component, use the architecture skill's frontmatter and section contract, then run `pnpm --filter @trilogy-ds/react check-docs`. Navigation is generated from this metadata; never maintain a separate component list.
2. Verify code changes before Figma synchronization: run the applicable Web and Native tests, type checks, documentation validation, style and story checks prescribed by the shared skills, and report failures or limitations. Build a verifiable inventory from the resulting code of UI props actually supported: names, values, defaults, variants, visual states, composable parts, and token mappings. Distinguish purely functional props and do not expose them as Figma UI properties. A prop with both visual and functional effects may have a visual representation without reproducing its functional logic.
   - Treat `CommonProps.style` as a code-only consumer customization escape hatch, not as a Figma property or design variant. Preserve it in React and do not attempt to map arbitrary CSS/React Native style objects into Figma.
3. Check differences between Web and Native, between code and Figma, and between tokens and their values. A difference between the verified code and an existing Figma design is normally the reason to update Figma, not a reason to block code-first work. If Web and Native differ materially and the design reference is unclear, present the differences and ask which platform or variant to represent rather than silently choosing. Ask before an incompatible or destructive Figma change; do not create unverified states or mappings.
4. Load the official Figma guides relevant to code-to-design: `figma-generate-design`, `figma-use`, and `figma-generate-library` for reusable components. For the first capture of a Web page, follow applicable capture and construction instructions; a capture is not an editable component and does not replace component creation. When updating a page already captured, modify the existing design rather than unnecessarily recreating it.
5. Load and follow [design-figma](../design-figma/SKILL.md) to identify the target file, open or reuse the Figma session, search for the component and semantic variables, create or update the component on its dedicated page, and validate bindings and rendering. Code is the source of truth for this task; do not modify an external library or destructively change an existing contract without approval. If a semantic variable or font is missing, follow that skill's blocker rule.
   - Create or reuse Figma main components for inventoried subcomponents on the same page as their family. When a representative composition is confirmed by code or usage examples, include **instances** of these subcomponents in the parent component or a visible assembly example, according to Figma capabilities and the component API. For example, show `AlertTitle` and `AlertDescription` in an `Alert`, optionally through `AlertContent`, and represent `ButtonList` with `Button` instances when consistent with usage. Do not invent composition or functional behavior: children in Figma illustrate React composition and do not imply that the React parent renders them automatically.
   - Preserve editable content and, where relevant and supported, instance UI properties. Reuse existing components and retain variants and semantic bindings; do not flatten instances into detached layers. If integration in the parent is unsafe or unsupported, retain reusable subcomponents and show an assembly example on the page; report the limitation.
6. Verify every inventoried item: main component, subcomponents, UI properties, structure and composition instances, values and defaults, variants, semantic variables, modes, and rendering. Provide Figma links for the parent and subcomponents and explicitly identify anything omitted, blocked, or unverified. Report code changes, differences or limitations, and tests run; do not present a screenshot or blocked step as a complete synchronization. If Figma access or another design prerequisite is unavailable, retain the completed code and report the Figma blocker instead of abandoning the code phase or claiming synchronization succeeded.
